findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. That covers the "what" and the "why" in a few sentences.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: This is Athena's home page, but the title and most of the body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer may wonder whose site they are on until they read the second paragraph.

The second section is a visible failure. The page has just promised a commit traceable to models, cost and verdict, and the one place meant to show that has nothing. This weakens the main pitch, and the internal error text leaks onto the page.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: There is a clear path forward: a link near the top, a clone command, prerequisites, ./setup.sh and a one-line example request (athena ask "add a changelog"). A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The steps don't say whether a Rust toolchain is needed, even though the page calls Athena a Rust system and lists a C linker. They also don't say which repository "your repository" means, presumably the current directory. A first-time installer may get stuck on either point.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" / "press Enter to run it on your repository"

findings.text: This link is aimed at the site owner, not a visitor. A newcomer may think it asks them to decide something.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The firstmate study is carefully built for a stranger: plain terms are defined before use, there is a step-by-step walk through one task, and it says openly where the source is silent (for example, 'in scope' and 'captain call'). As a demonstration of reading unfamiliar code, it is convincing.

Most of the page is a dense state-machine description with exit codes, guards and 45 cited claims. A newcomer evaluating Athena gets little from this, and nothing points them past it to the Next steps at the bottom.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t2: "lock contention or an unreadable capacity declaration refuses with exit 1 and does not wait"; Claims and sources (45 claims)

findings.text: This refers to an internal repository layout that a newcomer has not seen and has no reason to need.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
